title: Deep Neck Space Infections and Quinsy: Airway Risk and Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult deep neck space infection and peritonsillar abscess (quinsy): airway-risk recognition, imaging, drainage, antibiotics and referral, from an Indian national workflow and an Australian hospital guideline. Saudi-source review completed on 18 October 2026: The Saudi MOH protocol catalogue was reviewed but no opened Saudi deep-neck-space-infection or quinsy protocol with airway, imaging, drainage and antimicrobial details was identified. No Saudi endorsement of the existing doses is implied.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi national or NICE guideline for deep neck space infection or quinsy was opened.
The ICMR workflow names antibiotic classes but gives no doses; doses come only from the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital guideline (Australian practice).
The Eye and Ear guideline's dexamethasone wording is unclear, so no steroid regimen is given.
Metronidazole 12-hourly is as printed in the Australian source; check the hospital formulary.
SFDA registration of the listed antibiotics was not verified.
No paediatric dosing is included; this topic is adult only.

The Saudi MOH protocol catalogue was reviewed but no opened Saudi deep-neck-space-infection or quinsy protocol with airway, imaging, drainage and antimicrobial details was identified. No Saudi endorsement of the existing doses is implied.
The existing airway-risk, imaging, drainage and antimicrobial content was preserved as internationally sourced pending an opened Saudi ENT, emergency or antimicrobial-stewardship protocol.

pathophysiology.summary: Infection from a tonsil, tooth or pharynx can spread into deep neck spaces: submandibular (Ludwig's angina), peritonsillar, parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal. Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is pus collecting beside the tonsil and bulges the soft palate, deviating the uvula away from the abscess. Swelling narrows the airway; spread can reach the carotid sheath space, the prevertebral space and the anterior mediastinum. Complications include mediastinitis, necrotising fasciitis, venous thrombosis and lower cranial nerve palsy.

symptoms: Unilateral throat or ear pain, painful and difficult swallowing, poor oral intake.
Failure to respond to first-line oral antibiotics.
physicalSigns: Foul breath, trismus and asymmetrical bulging of the soft palate with the uvula pushed to the opposite side.
Tachycardia, fever and hypotension suggest systemic sepsis.
redFlags: Stridor, reduced consciousness or oxygen desaturation: possible complete airway obstruction.
Voice change: possible spread down to the larynx.
Severe sore throat and difficulty swallowing with stridor and no tonsillitis: treat as acute epiglottitis until proven otherwise.
Skin crepitus, discolouration or blisters (necrotising fasciitis), toxaemia, lower cranial nerve palsy, facial puffiness (venous thrombosis) or mediastinal extension.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Severe sore throat and dysphagia with stridor but no tonsillitis or pharyngitis; secure the airway first.
Needle aspiration finds no pus; the quinsy is confirmed when pus is aspirated.
Suspect when imaging or the clinical picture does not fit simple quinsy; confirm with contrast computed tomography (CT) of the neck.
Consider in patients over 50 with a suspicious presentation; arrange specialist follow-up in 2 weeks.

clinicalManagement.title: Secure the airway first
actions: Assess for stridor, reduced consciousness and desaturation.

If present, involve an anaesthetist or ENT on site to secure the airway, and arrange immediate ambulance transfer to a tertiary hospital with ENT and intensive care unit (ICU) or high-dependency unit (HDU) capability (Eye and Ear p. 2).
ICMR advises cautious airway assessment; intubate or consider tracheotomy if the airway is compromised, and secure the airway early in progressive disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess for spread and image
clinicalManagement.timeframe: First hour after the airway is safe
actions: Examine for trismus, uvular deviation, neck stiffness, crepitus, cranial nerve palsy and facial swelling.
Request FNE if the voice has changed.
Arrange contrast CT neck if parapharyngeal abscess is suspected, or if the patient is not improving or drainage has failed.
Treat hypotension with tachycardia and fever as sepsis, with fluids.

clinicalManagement.title: Drain the collection
actions: Needle aspiration by an experienced clinician: 21G or 18G needle about 1.5 cm deep, never pointed laterally because of the internal carotid artery.
Incision and drainage: infiltrate the anterior pillar with lidocaine 2% with adrenaline 1:80,000, incise with a size 15 blade, widen with curved artery forceps.
Peritonsillar abscesses are drained intraorally; other deep neck abscesses are drained externally (ICMR).
Drain urgently for airway compromise, mediastinal spread, vascular complication, necrotising fasciitis, deterioration over 24 hours or no response to antibiotics over 48–72 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics and admission
actions: Admit for overnight intravenous antibiotics, fluids and analgesia.
Adults: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV four times daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly; if penicillin allergic, clindamycin 450 mg IV three times daily.
Switch to oral after significant improvement: amoxicillin with clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily, or clindamycin 450 mg three times daily if penicillin allergic; total course 7 days (IV plus oral).
Consider delaying antibiotics until pus is sent for culture (Eye and Ear p. 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation and follow-up
actions: Refer to ENT for mediastinal spread, necrotising fasciitis, venous thrombosis or lower cranial nerve palsy.
First episode: general practitioner follow-up. Recurrent quinsy: head and neck clinic for elective tonsillectomy.
Age over 50 with a suspicious presentation: specialist follow-up within 2 weeks.
Treat the primary source (tonsil or tooth).

regimens.indication: Peritonsillar abscess or deep neck infection: initial intravenous therapy
regimens.duration: Until significant improvement, then oral step-down; 7 days in total
adjustments: No renal or hepatic adjustment is given in the source; check the hospital formulary.
monitoring: Reassess for significant improvement before switching IV to oral.
contraindications: Penicillin allergy: use the clindamycin regimen.

medicationPlan.note: Doses are from the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital guideline (adults only). The ICMR workflow lists penicillin, an aminoglycoside and metronidazole or clindamycin without doses. SFDA registration was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Stridor, reduced consciousness or desaturation (Eye and Ear p. 2).
Contrast CT neck if parapharyngeal abscess is suspected, or if there is no improvement or drainage has failed (Eye and Ear pp. 3–4).
Abscess formation, no response to antibiotics over 48–72 hours, deterioration over 24 hours, airway compromise, mediastinal spread, vascular complication or necrotising fasciitis.

guidelineComparison.title: ICMR neck space workflow versus Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital quinsy guideline

values: Contrast CT head and neck is standard; lateral neck X-ray or ultrasound if CT unavailable.
Contrast CT neck if parapharyngeal abscess is suspected or if there is no improvement or drainage has failed.
Early IV crystalline penicillin plus aminoglycoside plus metronidazole or clindamycin; no doses stated.
Benzylpenicillin plus metronidazole IV, or clindamycin if penicillin allergic; doses stated.
Peritonsillar abscess intraorally; other abscesses externally.
Needle aspiration or incision and drainage; tonsillectomy only electively for recurrence.
Single IV dexamethasone mentioned; wording unclear, so not adopted here.

learningObjectives: Recognise airway threat before any other task.
Choose imaging and drainage according to the space involved.
pitfalls: Delaying airway control to obtain imaging.
Treating severe sore throat with stridor and no tonsillitis as simple pharyngitis.
Missing mediastinal spread or necrotising fasciitis.
keyPoints: Stridor, desaturation or reduced consciousness need immediate airway control.
Contrast CT neck is the standard scan.
Needle must never be angled laterally during aspiration.

patientEducation: Return urgently for drooling, difficulty breathing, voice change, neck swelling or inability to open the mouth.
Finish the full antibiotic course (7 days in total).
Explain that worsening breathing, swallowing, voice change, drooling, neck swelling or inability to open the mouth needs emergency reassessment immediately.
lifestyleAndDiet: Maintain oral fluids and soft diet while swallowing is painful.
Dental review if a dental source is suspected.
mdtReferrals: ENT for drainage and airway; anaesthesia for airway control; ICU or HDU for airway compromise; dental surgery if dental source; head and neck clinic for recurrent quinsy.
dischargeCriteria: Significant clinical improvement and tolerating oral intake.
Safe airway with no stridor, drooling or progressive swelling.
Pus drained or collection excluded, and IV antibiotics stepped down to oral.
